notes:
I've arranged these notes verse by verse. The Protestant disagreements are at vv. 7, 9–10, 10, 18 and 21. **Gaps:** I didn't find anything from a Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran or specifically Pentecostal source, nothing from netbible.org, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so none of those appear below. Haydock's Catholic commentary is listed on Bible Hub, but I didn't open it. A few points below come from full pages I opened that can't be cited line by line; those have the URL only.

---

**v. 1**
- "Precious" in older translations means *rare*. "The word of the LORD" means God's will announced through a prophet, seer or man of God. Ellicott thinks no inspired voice had spoken between Deborah and the unnamed man of God who came to Eli. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-3.html 
- The Pulpit Commentary says there was no regular group of prophets God could speak through. It sees Samuel as the founder of prophecy as an established office, and prophet, priest and king as three roles that prepare for Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Gill (Baptist) says there was no publicly known prophet people could go to for guidance, though God may still have spoken privately to individuals. He also says this rarity explains why Samuel, and even Eli at first, didn't recognise the voice.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/3-1.html
- Guzik says the only "word of the LORD" in chapters 1–2 is the judgment brought by the man of God, so when God did speak, it was judgment. He blames the people's hard hearts and the corrupt priesthood.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- MacLaren pictures a corrupt priesthood, a people turned away and a silent God, with Samuel's quiet service as the contrast. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/3-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Eli's dim eyes describe him spiritually as well as physically. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Pulpit: Samuel was probably about 12 (Josephus) and looked after the failing Eli. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Bible.org: Eli's age, weight and poor sight meant he needed a boy like Samuel to run errands for him.  https://bible.org/seriespage/4-rise-samuel-and-fall-eli-and-sons-1-samuel-31-422

**v. 3**
- The lamp burned through the night and went out around daybreak, so the call came in the dark early hours.  https://bible.org/seriespage/4-rise-samuel-and-fall-eli-and-sons-1-samuel-31-422
- Some readers take the lamp as the "lamp of prophecy": before it went out in Eli, it was lit in Samuel. Ellicott quotes a Talmud saying that God never takes one righteous man away before another is born.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/3-3.html,  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/3.htm
- Gill: the ark was in the holy of holies, God's dwelling place, and mentioning it shows where the voice came from. Samuel probably slept close to Eli.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/3-3.html
- MacLaren and Guzik both read the scene as a picture of Israel: dark, perhaps getting darker, but the lamp not yet out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/3-1.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/

**v. 4**
- Ellicott thinks the voice probably came from the visible glory (the Shekinah) resting on the mercy seat over the ark.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-3.html
- Guzik thinks the voice was probably audible, though he isn't certain. "Here I am" puts Samuel alongside Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Isaiah and Ananias.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Precept Austin: we can't be sure whether this was a dream or vision, but Samuel heard a voice and answered aloud.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-3-commentary

**vv. 5–6**
- Matthew Henry sees Samuel's quickness as a model for servants and for the young caring for the old.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_003.cfm
- Guzik: Samuel was mistaken about who called, but right to hurry, because he knew Eli was blind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Precept Austin: Eli not catching on the second time is a sign of his dulled spiritual sight.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-3-commentary
- MacLaren draws a lesson both ways: we mistake God's voice for a man's, and also a man's voice for God's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/3-1.htm

**v. 7 — Protestant teachers differ: did Samuel already know God personally?**
- **Not yet saved.** Bible.org (evangelical) says Samuel was not yet saved when called and was saved during the encounter, like Paul. The difference from Eli's sons is the word "yet."  https://bible.org/seriespage/4-rise-samuel-and-fall-eli-and-sons-1-samuel-31-422
- **Not yet converted.** Guzik (enduringword.com) says Samuel was godly but hadn't yet given his heart to the LORD; even children of godly homes must be converted by the Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- **Knew God, but not as one who speaks.** The Pulpit Commentary says Samuel knew God in conscience and spiritual life, unlike Eli's sons, but not yet as one who reveals his will to people.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- **Same view in Gill.** Gill (Baptist) says Samuel already had spiritual knowledge of God; what he lacked was a word of prophecy. The Targum reads it the same way.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/1-samuel-3.html (this is a Spanish translation of Gill)
- **Same view in Matthew Henry.** Samuel knew the written word, but the way God speaks to prophets was new to him.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_003.cfm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: Eli was experienced enough to realise the third time that this was God. He may have remembered the man of God's warning.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Matthew Henry (Reformed): God keeps repeating a call that grace means to make effective until it succeeds.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_003.cfm

**v. 9 — teachers differ on applying this to hearing God today**
- Guzik takes the repeated calls as a principle: God usually confirms what he says, and acting dramatically on a single "inner voice" is generally wrong.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- In Guzik's reading, Eli's advice teaches four things: be available, don't presume God will speak, respond, and be humble. Other voices count for nothing eternally unless God speaks through them.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Seedbed (Wesleyan) applies it more directly to daily life. The writer says the Lord is always speaking, and the word is rare today because we don't ask and don't listen. Samuel's words are offered as a daily prayer.  https://seedbed.com/speak-lord-for-your-servant-is-listening/
- Precept Austin: recognising God's call isn't always easy, and Eli acted faithfully as a witness here.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-3-commentary
- Pulpit: Eli sent Samuel back to bed because obedience and trusting submission are the best preparation for hearing God.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Ligonier (Reformed) finds it sad that Eli taught Samuel to listen while not listening to God himself.  https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-calls-samuel
- Matthew Henry: put good words into children's mouths early.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_003.cfm

**v. 10 — teachers differ on what "came and stood" means**
- **Possibly Christ.** Guzik says this may have been a unique appearance of the LORD, perhaps Jesus before Bethlehem, and not a dream.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- **A personal presence.** Precept Austin says it implies God's personal presence, as when the Angel of the LORD stood before others.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-3-commentary
- **Form not described.** Ellicott notes that other appearances say what form God took; this one doesn't.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/3.htm
- **Seen while awake.** The Pulpit Commentary says this was an objective presence seen by someone fully awake, not a trance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- **Seen inwardly.** MacLaren says the sight was to the "inward eye." Because Eli heard nothing, he thinks the voice, though real, probably wasn't audible to the senses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/3-1.htm
- **The double name.** Matthew Henry says calling the name twice shows God's delight, and that Samuel would now understand.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_003.cfm. A source quoted on Precept Austin calls it God's "double knock," like "Simon, Simon" and "Saul, Saul."  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-3-commentary
- **Wesleyan application.** For Seedbed, this moment begins Israel's great prophetic tradition.  https://seedbed.com/speak-lord-for-your-servant-is-listening/

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the event that makes ears tingle is the capture of the ark, which seemed to say God had abandoned Israel.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/3.htm
- Pulpit: the Hebrew is closer to "I am doing," since the ruin is already under way. The same phrase is later used of Jerusalem's fall.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-3.html
- Bible.org: this is no exaggeration, since Eli collapses and dies when he hears the news (4:18).  https://bible.org/seriespage/4-rise-samuel-and-fall-eli-and-sons-1-samuel-31-422

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: "carry out" is literally "raise up," meaning God wakes up the threats spoken in 2:27 that had been lying dormant. "From beginning to end" translates two Hebrew infinitives.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-3.html
- Guzik: this confirms the earlier warning, and Spurgeon notes that God has many messengers, a child among them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/

**v. 13**
- **Textual note (Pulpit).** The verb normally means "cursed," and "cursed themselves" reads awkwardly. The Septuagint (the ancient Greek Old Testament) reads "God" instead of "themselves"; Buxtorf lists this among places where scribes changed "me" to "themselves." Pulpit itself translates "brought a curse upon themselves." The BSB's "blasphemed God" follows the "God" reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Pulpit: Eli should have removed his sons from office.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-3.html
- Ellicott: the priests' example spread unbelief through all Israel, yet Eli still didn't remove them.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/3.htm
- Guzik: Eli's duty was mainly as their superior, the high priest over priests, since they were adults. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- MacLaren: someone who tolerates evil he's responsible for stopping becomes an accomplice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/3-1.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: neither animal sacrifice (*zebach*) nor grain offering (*minchah*) could cover this guilt, because the sons hardened themselves after the warning in 2:27–36.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-3.html
- Bible.org: they have passed the point of no return.  https://bible.org/seriespage/4-rise-samuel-and-fall-eli-and-sons-1-samuel-31-422
- Guzik applies it today: the only sin beyond atonement is rejecting Jesus' sacrifice (Heb 10:26).  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Gill: legal sacrifices could only atone symbolically anyway, and the high priesthood never returned to Eli's family. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/1-samuel-3.html

**v. 15**
- The doors show that permanent buildings had grown up around the Tabernacle.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-3.html
- Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship) agrees that Shiloh had become a more permanent structure.  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/shiloh/
- Pulpit: being trusted with the keys suggests Samuel was no longer a small child. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Ellicott calls this Samuel's first taste of the prophet's cross: telling hard truth to people he loved.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/3.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- "My son" shows real affection between them. Pulpit says Eli's oath effectively put Samuel under oath, so hiding anything would have been perjury.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Guzik: Samuel was Eli's "second chance" at raising a son.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Precept Austin: in a time when God's word was rare, Eli was eager to hear it.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-3-commentary

**v. 18 — teachers really differ on Eli's response**
- **Praised as submission.** A. W. Pink (on monergism.com, Reformed) calls it wonderful submission and an example of grace controlling the heart's strongest feelings.  https://www.monergism.com/blog/entire-resignation-gods-sovereignty
- **Proof he was a good man.** The Puritan Edmund Calamy says the way Eli accepted his punishment shows he was good, despite his great fault.  https://www.monergism.com/eli-trembling-ark-god-1-samuel-413
- **Criticised.** Ligonier (also Reformed) says resignation was the wrong response; God relents when people repent, and Eli's failure to ask for mercy shows spiritual lethargy.  https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-calls-samuel
- **Undecided.** Guzik says it's hard to tell whether this was godly or fatalistic. True submission is also active: it repents. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- **Older Anglican commentaries are positive.** Pulpit says his humility shows the Holy Spirit had been working on him.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm. Ellicott says Eli was devoted to the Lord at heart, though it was probably too late to reform the priesthood.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/3.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** uses Eli's words as a model for grieving believers who must bow to God's will.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/sermons/2893.cfm

**v. 19**
- "None of his words fall to the ground" means all of Samuel's prophecies came true.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Ellicott contrasts the grown Samuel with Eli.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-3.html

**v. 20**
- "From Dan to Beersheba" means the whole country, which shows a sense of being one people even in the anarchy of the judges' time. "Confirmed" is the same word used of Moses in Numbers 12:7, meaning both faithful and established.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Guzik: Samuel was Israel's last judge and first prophet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Matthew Henry, quoted by Ligonier: God never leaves his church without a guide.  https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-calls-samuel
- Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship): Samuel is never explicitly called a priest. The "faithful priest" promised in 2:35 seems, from the context, to be Samuel, and 3:20 is the first time he is called a prophet.  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/samuel/

**v. 21**
- **Christ the Word?** Gill takes "word of the LORD" as possibly Christ appearing in human form.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/1-samuel-3.html. Pulpit notes that many older commentators read it as the second person of the Trinity, but thinks it simply means prophetic inspiration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/3.htm
- Guzik: whenever God moves, he reveals himself by his word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-3/
- Bible Odyssey: Shiloh was the main place of worship until Samuel's time, then largely drops out of the story after the ark was captured.  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/shiloh/,  https://biblehub.bibleodyssey.org/articles/shiloh/

**Background (other views)**
- **Samaritan reading of Eli.** In Samaritan tradition, Eli is judged for leaving Mount Gerizim and setting up an illegitimate priesthood at Shiloh.  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/eli/
- **Samuel's name.** The meaning is unclear; suggestions include "Heard of God."  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/samuel/
